This is essential reporting by Doug MacMillan at The Washington Post. Earlier this year I sat down with Doug to talk about how he investigates ICE detention. You can watch our full conversation here.

austinkocher.substack.com/p/investigat...
This investigation draws on ICE facility population data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through Freedom of Information Act requests and analyzed by The Washington Post.

At a Dallas hold room in March, a 41-year-old Afghan man who fought alongside U.S. troops called his brother to say he had chest pain and staff were ignoring his requests for care. He died hours later after being rushed to a hospital.

The pattern did not stay in New York. Since last August, eight other temporary hold rooms have held more than 200 people at once, agency data shows. At Arizona’s Mesa Gateway Airport, ICE packed more than 700 people into a facility built for 203.
On August 12 a federal judge capped 26 Federal Plaza at 22 people total across all four holding rooms, warning of “a very serious threat of continuing irreparable injury.”

Daniel Quevedo Silva, a Venezuelan man arrested leaving his court hearing, spent nine days confined with more than 70 other men. “The officers gave us aluminum-type blankets but I was freezing the entire time,” he said in court testimony.

There were no doctors on site. Officials triaged detainees with serious conditions using nicknames like “cardiac lady.” “Cardiac lady? We don’t have her meds it’s becoming an issue,” assistant field office director Nancy Zanello texted her boss.

ICE officials warned each other for weeks. “We desperately need to get some detainees out of 26 fed,” assistant field office director Carla Calidonio wrote to colleagues on June 14. “Is anything being done at all?”

Federal policy limited these temporary rooms to 12 hours. On June 24 ICE changed its own policy to allow three days. Before the surge the longest stay was 21 hours. In June and July more than 60 people were held there for over a week.

Hold Room 1 is about 30 feet on each side, with hard floors, concrete benches, three metal toilets, and no beds or showers. At its most crowded each person had about 10 square feet of space, roughly the size of a phone booth.
